Work / MS 360
01 — Complex Systems · HP Inc.

MS 360 — Printer Fleet Management Ecosystem

Senior Product Designer / Product Lead · Phase 1, 8–12 months
RoleProduct Designer & Product Lead
TeamPM, 6–8 engineers, data eng, QA
Timeline8–12 months (Phase 1)
ToolsRetool, Figma, HP Veneer DS
Background

Telemetry everywhere, answers nowhere.

Large HP printer fleets throw off continuous telemetry — device diagnostics, usage metrics, service alerts, billing data — at a density and scale most consumer products never touch. That data sat scattered across legacy operational, financial, and technical systems, each with its own constraints and access rules.

We built MS 360 as three purpose-built applications sharing one event and data layer, with access scoped by role across L1–L3 support tiers, finance, and executive users.

The three applications

One data layer, three jobs to be done.

EMS

Event Management System

Purpose

Defines event rules and governs severity classification so every alert means the same thing everywhere.

Primary users

System administrators, service engineers, fleet ops teams.

Outcome

Events stay consistently classified and easy to audit, instead of duplicated per system.

CC 360

Command Center 360

Purpose

A centralised dashboard where service agents investigate issues across accounts, fleets, and individual assets.

Primary users

Service agents, technical support, fleet operations.

Outcome

Agents identify device failures, print-quality issues, firmware problems, and maintenance triggers faster.

CXE 360

Financial & Contract Insights

Purpose

Gives leadership real-time visibility into service revenue and contractual performance.

Primary users

HP executives, finance teams, business managers.

Outcome

Decision-makers see service profitability as it happens instead of waiting on static reports.

Discovery

Who I designed for.

We ran stakeholder interviews with service agents and operations managers, observed live incident triage, reviewed historical service incidents, and audited the existing monitoring tools before drawing a single screen.

CC 360

Service Agent

Monitors device health, investigates alerts, runs remote diagnostics Pain points
  • Correlating data across disconnected systems
  • Slow, multi-step investigation workflows
Goal
  • One place to diagnose and resolve a case
EMS

System Administrator

Owns event definitions, severity levels, rule performance Pain points
  • Fragmented rule management
  • Duplicate event definitions
Goal
  • Standardised, governed event classification
CXE 360

Business Stakeholder

Tracks financial performance and contract profitability Pain points
  • Financial data scattered across reports
  • Delayed insight into service performance
Goal
  • Fast, comparable business metrics

Storyboard

Six sheets of paper, before any pixels.

Every console screen started as a pencil sheet. Paper kept the conversation with service engineers about structure — what sits next to what, and what has to be visible at once — rather than about colour. Sheet 02 is the one that became the contracts console in the comparison above.

Design system

Working inside Veneer, not beside it.

MS 360 didn't get its own visual language. HP runs Veneer — the company's software design system, which gives UI designers, developers and UX writers a shared set of components, design tokens, icons and writing guidelines so products across very different business units still feel like one company. Three new applications were exactly the situation Veneer exists to prevent going wrong.

300+ Teams on the system

Veneer is the most widely adopted design system HP has produced, spanning a company with more than a hundred product lines.

~50% Faster development

HP's own measured benchmark for building with the system rather than from scratch — in line with published industry findings.

915 Icon components

Used by 320 teams at roughly 85,000 insertions a week — the scale that makes reinventing an icon set indefensible.

Figures published by HP's design system team via veneer.hp.com, the Figma Dev Mode case study, and the 2025 UX Design Awards entry. They describe Veneer's org-wide impact, not this project's.

What the system gave us
  • Components, design tokens, iconography and writing guidance, already accessibility-reviewed
  • A visual language HP service teams recognised from other internal tools, so nothing needed re-learning
  • Design-to-code parity maintained centrally, which kept handoff arguments off the table
What still had to be solved
  • Reconciling Retool's stock component set with Veneer's specification — the build platform and the design language did not start aligned
  • Dense operational tables and telemetry views that sit beyond what a general-purpose component library anticipates
  • Holding one navigation shell steady across three apps serving support engineers, finance and executives

The spec written on top of it

Veneer set the language. These pages pinned it down for MS 360 specifically — the exact ramps, states and components three teams had to build against.

Primary colours

Electric Blue, white and black as the core set — Electric Blue carries interaction and draws attention to key information.

Colour progression

A consistent grey ramp so Electric Blue and black can define interaction states predictably.

Background usage

White as the default background for space and clarity; light grey as the base layer beneath open layouts.

Text usage

Black as the core text colour with grey for hierarchy, shown at the weights actually used.

Functional colours

Error, pending, success and warning specified across background, icon and text so status reads the same everywhere.

Component — global header

The header spec as applied to CC 360: product switching, tabs, and the overview/detail split.

Component — titles & tabs

Type sizes and weights pinned per level, so three teams building three apps produce the same headings.

Component — sidebar

The sidebar as primary navigation: every console page with its icon, plus relevant external links.

Information architecture

Three apps, one navigation shell.

With three products sharing a shell, the real design problem was navigation: where does a service agent go versus a system admin versus an executive? I mapped the module structure before any visual design started.

MS 360 — global shell
CC 360
  • Asset / Fleet / Account
  • Incidents & connectivity
  • Consumables & service requests
  • Onboarding
CXE 360
  • Executive summary
  • Invoice accuracy & trends
  • Dispute ageing
  • Contracts & devices
EMS
  • Event definitions & correlations
  • Live events
  • Missing definitions
  • Rules playground
ArtifactInformation architecture mapThe full navigation model: utility, global, primary and secondary levels across all three apps.

Utility navigation sits outside the hierarchy (global search, punch-out links, my task, activity history, global header, sidebar, notification centre, AI chat). Below it, three apps branch into their own primary and secondary trees — CC 360 into asset, fleet and account; EMS into event definitions, correlations and rules; CXE 360 into onboarding, executive and account.

Final UI

The shipped consoles.

MS 360 is desktop software for people who sit in it all day, so the layouts are wide and dense by design — filters, tables and detail panels held in one view rather than split across pages. These are shipped screens at full width, across all three applications.

MS 360Unify — the landing console

One view, better context. The entry point routes to the onboarding dashboard (TMC and JIRA workflows, project stages, SLA performance, deployment status) and to the executive dashboard for team, country and global performance.

CC 360Explore assets

Serial-number and device search as the front door — the fastest path from a support ticket to the asset it concerns.

CC 360Contracts and devices

The console agents live in: contracts, devices, request items and invoicing across one filter set, with overview and detailed views per asset.

CC 360Asset detail

A single asset in full — entitlement and operational status, ITSM linkage, connectivity, incidents, locations and contacts. Customer identifiers are blurred here.

CC 360Consumables and fulfilment

Toner, drum, transfer kit and waste collector levels against threshold limits, with open fulfilment needs and collection dates.

EMSEvent Management System — overview

The rules layer: definitions, correlations, live events, missing definitions and a rules playground, each as its own workspace.

EMSEvent definitions

Definitions grouped by parent with lifecycle state, last occurrence, source, category, type and sub-type — the table that decides what an alert means.

EMSCorrelations

Where related raw events are grouped into one meaningful incident instead of firing separately.

EMSLive events

The running feed — print-quality diagnostics, engine analysis and expert rules resolving in real time.

Executive consoleInvoice overview

Invoice accuracy and timeliness against target, with dispute volume — the numbers leadership opens first.

Executive consoleDetailed view

The same picture filtered by region, country, business, model type and account, for when the headline number needs explaining.

Executive consoleAccount dashboard

A single account end to end — contracts, devices, request items and invoicing in one place.

Executive consoleMaster agreements

Agreement status by region, country and business model, with summary rollups.

My role

Designer and product lead, in parallel.

As Senior UX/UI Designer
  • Ran discovery with service teams and stakeholders
  • Wireframed dashboards and structured the information hierarchy
  • Designed search and investigation flows for accounts, fleets, and assets
  • Partnered with engineering to keep every design build-feasible
As Product Lead
  • Identified gaps in event-definition management and documented agent pain points
  • Aligned finance stakeholders, PMs, and engineering on scope
  • Structured the product ecosystem into clear, discoverable modules
  • Contributed documentation that kept design, product, and engineering in sync
Impact

What changed.

Agent efficiency

Service agents identify issues faster, with far less time lost navigating between platforms.

Event governance

Structured definitions and severity mapping made incident triage manageable across thousands of assets.

Fleet visibility

Teams can proactively monitor fleet health and catch problems before they escalate.

Financial clarity

Executives get a consolidated, real-time view of billing and contract performance.
